Older designs of this kind covered only flat, two-dimensional areas. They also served ground users only, or worked in a passive mode with no boost. A boosted signal helps beat the fading that hits a signal twice on its path. The design aims to do all this while using energy with care.
arxiv-2601-17851:
Hua Yue, Lin Nie, Yiqing Guo, and Hongbo Hu revisit a long-standing puzzle in cosmic ray physics. Their 2026 preprint is about the knee, a bend in the cosmic ray energy spectrum. No one yet knows for sure what makes the bend. Guesses point to how the rays are sped up, how they hit other matter, or how they spread through the Galaxy.

New data give the team fresh leverage. The LHAASO observatory has measured the proton spectrum with fine care, along with total and composition spectra and the rays' direction spread. By testing models against all of these at once, the authors narrow where the knee's cause can sit. Joint use of spectrum and direction is the key move.
arxiv-2601-17951:
Yuhan Wen and co-authors look for signs that black holes starve their own galaxies. Their 2026 preprint studies quasars with moderate radio output. An active galactic nucleus pours out energy that can heat cold gas or push it out of the galaxy. Cold gas is the raw stuff of new stars, so losing it can shut star birth down. The team asks how radio activity links to the size of those gas stores.

They compare quasars across levels of radio strength. If stronger radio output pairs with thinner gas, that is a clue that feedback is at work. The title reports evidence of gas depletion in these quasars. Such clues help piece together how black holes shape the growth of galaxies over time.
arxiv-2601-18051:
Mia Kumamoto and Catherine Welch compute how neutrinos interact inside merging neutron stars when strong magnetic fields are present. Their 2026 preprint deals with neutrino opacities, which set how far neutrinos travel before they scatter. Neutrinos shape both transport and flavor change in the debris of a merger. Simulations hint that mergers can build fields as strong as 10^17 gauss. Yet computing field effects on interaction rates has been too hard to include.

The authors take on that computation directly. Better rates change how merger models predict heat, composition, and the light we see. Those predictions feed the study of how heavy elements form. The work removes a known gap in merger physics.
arxiv-2601-18251:
Kesha Ou and co-authors model how a user's interests shift over time, for better click prediction. Their 2026 preprint presents GenCI. Click-through rate prediction is pivotal in online ads and recommenders. Most models match a candidate item against the user's history. That matching can overfit to the traits that dominated the past. It then fails when interests move fast. The authors instead model interest shift in a generative way, learning intent through cohorts of similar users.

Cohort views let the model borrow strength from people with like patterns. A user whose taste is turning can be read against a cohort that already turned. Fresher intent reads should lift both ads and feeds.
arxiv-2601-18551:
Paloma Thevenet and four colleagues watch the jet of a far bright galaxy core twist and swing over time. The core, named 3C 66A, shoots a thin jet of stuff at near light speed. Shots from a world web of dishes can read the jet at fine scale, close to its root. More and more such jets are seen to change their aim with time.

That change of aim can hint at a wobble in the disc that feeds the core, or at shakes in the jet it-self. The team track the jet across many dates to chart its twist and swing. A clean chart helps sort which cause fits the moves. It also feeds the tale of how cores and their discs dance as one. Such work needs long, calm watch over years.
arxiv-2601-18751:
Seyed Amir Hosseini and six colleagues tackle a flaw in a way to teach agents from side-by-side picks. In that path, a judge says which of two runs was best, and the agent learns from the pick. Real judges are a mixed lot. Some are sharp, some are sloppy, and some pick the worst run on aim. Past tools treat all picks the same, or try to drop the bad judges out.

Both paths fail when a judge is sly: their picks look like help but push the agent wrong. The team build a tool that can trust, doubt, or flip each judge's picks as it learns. A flipped pick from a sly judge turns from harm to help. Such care could make pick-based training safe in the wild, where judges can't all be vetted.
arxiv-2601-19051:
Henry Chen and four co-authors harden language model systems by attacking them first, on purpose. Prompt based attacks are a chief risk when such systems go live, since user input is free form text with no fixed shape. Guards built once tend to age fast as attack tricks evolve.

Their system, HASTE, keeps forging fresh attack vectors and uses them to tune the defense while the system runs. It was shared at a security workshop tied to the NDSS symposium. A defense that trains against new attacks as they emerge fits a threat that never stands still.
arxiv-2601-19451:
Isha Pandey and three co-authors give speech recognition a team of projectors for many languages at once. New systems link frozen speech encoders to language models through light projector layers. In one language that works well, but a single projector strains to map the diverse sounds of many languages into meaning.

Their method uses dynamic multi expert projectors with stabilized routing, so each language leans on the experts that fit it. Speech tools that hold up across languages serve the many users whom English only systems leave behind. Stable routing keeps the team from collapsing onto a few overused experts.
arxiv-2601-19551:
Geunhyeok Yu and Hyoseok Hwang take on a flaw in deep learning models that refine their answers step by step. Many models stack layers, and each layer updates an internal state. Yet nothing forces those middle states to stay meaningful. That gap makes early stopping and adaptive computing shaky, since a half-finished state may be nonsense.

The authors set a structural rule: the internal dynamics should stay scale-consistent across rounds of refinement. From that rule they derive a method called FROST. It gives the state space a self-similar, fractal-like structure through a built-in bias. With that structure, partial results are more likely to be valid on their own. The work aims at models that can stop early and still be trusted.
arxiv-2601-19851:
Rayna Hata and four colleagues study how blind people share control with a navigation robot. Independent navigation is vital to daily life but hard without sight. Robots can guide users and build confidence. Yet a fully autonomous robot can leave the user feeling sidelined, even when they want to stay involved.

The authors ask how delegation in this partnership evolves over time. Early trips may need heavy robot guidance. As trust and skill grow, the balance may shift. Their study follows that changing relationship. Designing for delegation means respecting the user's wish for control. The findings guide robots that assist without taking over.
arxiv-2601-20051:
Gautham Vinod and four colleagues recover the true size of food from a single photograph. Diet-related chronic diseases like obesity and diabetes make accurate food monitoring valuable. AI dietary tools can name foods in a photo. Estimating how much food is present, the portion, is the pressing challenge, because a flat image hides scale.

Their method reconstructs real-scale three-dimensional models from monocular images. True scale turns a picture into a portion estimate. That answers the question diet tracking actually asks: how much did you eat? The reconstruction must work from one ordinary photo, not a lab scan. Better portion estimates could make nutrition apps trustworthy enough for clinical use.
arxiv-2601-20251:
Skyler Wu, Yash Nair, and Emmanuel J. Candès make the evaluation of large language models cheaper while keeping statistical guarantees. Testing many models on a large suite of benchmarks is expensive, since each test item costs a model call. The authors cast benchmarking as finite-population inference, like surveying a fixed set of items.

Under a fixed query budget, they seek tight confidence intervals for model accuracy with valid coverage. Smart sampling can then rank models without testing every item. This matters as benchmark suites grow: labs could spend less on evaluation and still know how sure each ranking is.
arxiv-2601-20951:
Ashwat Jain, Wojciech Jankowski, M. Mehraeen, and Robert-Jan Slager show that some topological phases can steer sound in one direction. Their 2026 paper presents the topological acoustic diode. A diode lets a signal pass one way but not back. Here the signal is sound, and the gate is a three-dimensional topological phase. The team shows such phases realize nonlinear odd acoustoelastic effects.

Two effects stand out. One is anomalous acoustic second-harmonic generation, where sound doubles its frequency. The other is rectification, where vibration yields a steady response. Both are captured by a momentum-space tensor from quantum state geometry. The work joins topology with acoustics in a fresh way. It hints at devices that route or harvest sound using quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-21151:
Carlos Pereira and a large team of co-authors give weather models a dedicated engine for moving air. Their 2026 paper presents a neural semi-Lagrangian architecture for weather forecasting. Recent machine learning forecasters often use one monolithic network. Distinct physical mechanisms are then represented only implicitly. Advection, diffusion-like mixing, thermodynamics, and forcing all blur together. Advection suffers most from that blur. It needs long-range transport across the globe.

Treating advection implicitly demands expensive global interactions or deep convolutional stacks. A semi-Lagrangian design follows air parcels along their paths instead. That matches how the atmosphere actually moves weather. The architecture builds transport in, rather than hoping a big network learns it. The paper aims for forecasts that respect physics by construction. It joins a push for hybrid models that keep the best of both traditions.
arxiv-2601-21251:
Ce Hao, Xuanran Zhai, Yaohua Liu, and Harold Soh teach robots to reuse skills across many tasks. Policies based on diffusion models do well at single manipulation tasks. Extending them to many tasks usually needs much bigger models and far more demonstrations.

Their policy mixes a small set of expert parts that share a compact skill base. A sticky routing step picks a few fitting experts for each moment of a task. Skills learned for one job can then be combined for new ones. The design aims at robots that learn broad skills without a fresh giant model for every task.
arxiv-2601-21351:
Chendong Song and seven co-authors work out the best split between two kinds of hardware in serving language models. A new serving design separates attention work from the feed-forward work after it. Attention is heavy on memory, while the other part is heavy on raw compute.

The two pools are linked at each generation step, so balance matters. Too few units on either side leaves the other side idle and slows every token. The authors derive the ratio that should work best in theory. Their result gives operators a principled way to size each pool instead of guessing.
arxiv-2601-21551:
Yang Zhou and eight co-authors improve how language models take a patient's history over several turns of talk. Good history taking is a core clinical skill, yet it is rarely tested directly. Models shine on fixed quizzes but often falter in live, turn-by-turn diagnosis.

Their method feeds the model real medical notes to guide its questions. With the notes in view, the model can refine its guesses as answers arrive. Better questioning should lead to faster, safer diagnosis support. The work treats conversation itself, not just the final answer, as the skill to train.
arxiv-2601-21651:
Savvas Panagi, Chrysovalantis Spanias, and Petros Aristidou jointly optimize heat and power in local grids filled with electric cars and heat pumps. Electrifying transport and heating gives grid operators welcome flexibility. The same devices also tie thermal and electrical behavior tightly together.

That coupling breaks the assumptions of older network management. Their framework plans both sides at once for active distribution grids. Coordinated control can shave peaks by timing charging and heating against each other. The work supports towns adding many electric vehicles and heat pumps without rebuilding the whole network.
arxiv-2601-21951:
James Matthew Young and co-authors build samplers for probability distributions that are known only up to a scaling constant. Many problems in physics and statistics have exactly that form. Diffusion-based samplers move along a path that smoothly connects a simple starting distribution to the hard target one.

The team's 2026 preprint combines that diffusion path with sequential Monte Carlo. That method carries a population of samples. It reweights them along the way. The blend aims for samples that are both accurate and efficient to draw. Better samplers feed everything from Bayesian model fitting to molecular simulation. Where the quality of conclusions is capped by the quality of the samples behind them.
arxiv-2601-22051:
Nabhanila Nandi and co-authors study thin wires where two states of matter fight. The wires join a magnet to a material that can carry power with no loss. The magnet tends to kill that loss-free state. Yet the state can live on where the pull of the magnet fades or cancels out.

Near the walls that split one magnet zone from the next, the pull drops to near zero. The loss-free state can grow there. It can also grow when many small zones mix, so that their pulls average out to near zero. The team shows how the pattern of these zones shapes where the state can live. Such wires are a test bed for new types of quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-22351:
Richard Battye and Adam Moss ask a plain question: must dark energy push the same way in all directions? Dark energy drives the late growth of the cosmos. Their 2026 preprint lets the push vary by direction and by time, in a stretched-space model.

They shape the model so a key bound from the faint early glow holds by design. That bound comes from how the glow's heat shifts as it crosses space. The work maps how much warp the data still allow. It tests a core claim of the standard cosmic story.
arxiv-2601-22551:
Meixia Lin and a large team tackle camera location across mixed devices for the CroCoDL 2025 challenge. Their 2026 preprint joins a shared retrieval encoder with two paths to a fix. One path uses classic geometry with fused features and a PnP solve; the other is a neural feed-forward model fed with geometric inputs.

Cross-device location matters when phones, drones, and robots must share one map. A hybrid that pairs classic rigor with learned speed can hold up where either alone fails. The work is a contest entry, built to a shared test.
arxiv-2601-22651:
Naoki Murata and a team assign credit for a diffusion model's output to whole groups of training data. Attribution asks which data shaped a given image. Their 2026 preprint, Guda, notes that users often need group answers — a style, a class — not one image at a time.

Group credit is a counterfactual: how would the output change if the group were gone? Their method answers by way of unlearning. Fair group credit can guide pay, consent, and data curation. The work serves artists and data holders most. It makes a vague debt concrete.
arxiv-2601-22751:
Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan and Bum Jun Kim built a physics-informed network that reads off scaling exponents as it solves. Near singularities and critical points, nature follows power laws. Their 2026 preprint notes that standard networks hide those exponents inside their weights.

Their Müntz-Szász network treats the exponents as trainable dials. It outputs both the solution and its scaling shape. Known exponents let scholars check a result against theory at a glance. The work serves physics where the exponent is the story. It makes a hidden number explicit. Clear exponents also make results easy to share.
arxiv-2601-22951:
Mayank Nautiyal and seven co-authors present OneFlowSBI, one model that answers many inference questions. Simulation-based inference learns from computer simulations when direct formulas are out of reach. Usually each question, like finding likely parameters, needs its own training run.

Their model learns the joint pattern of parameters and observations in one go. A masking trick during training lets the same model sample posteriors, estimate likelihoods, and more. One flexible model could speed up science fields that lean on heavy simulators. Query-aware masking during training is the trick that lets one trained model serve many different inference questions afterward.
arxiv-2601-23151:
Katherine Keegan and Lars Ruthotto help AI models create samples that must obey strict rules. These models work well on many tasks. But they hit a wall when each sample must meet exact equal terms, as is common in science. The sample space then forms a curved surface, and naive sampling drifts off it.

Their fix bends the samples back toward that surface in a cheap and sound way. It is built to be flexible, so it can plug into many model types. The aim is to cure known flaws of rule-bound generation. Sound samples that respect hard rules serve design, physics, and other fields where a wrong sample is useless.
arxiv-2603-01451:
When epoxy resin hardens, tiny filler grains inside it can clump, and that clumping shapes how strong the final solid is. Yujiro Furuta and Rei Kurita study that change in this 2026 lab work. They ask if hardening by itself pulls grains together, even when no strong pull should exist.

The pair placed small glowing plastic beads in epoxy resin and set off hardening with a curing agent. A fine microscope let them map bead spots in three dimensions before and after the resin set. Clumping grew during curing, and the growth tracked the mean gap between beads, not just how full the mix was. That rule gives makers a way to guess the final spread of filler in paints, glues, and similar goods.
arxiv-2603-01651:
Anka Chandrahas Tummepalli and Preethu Rose Anish pull event timelines out of Indian Supreme Court judgments in this 2026 work. Court texts are long and unstructured, which limits how well AI tools can sum them up or predict outcomes. A clear timeline of who did what, and when, gives those tools firm ground.

Their frame, LexChronos, pairs two agents in a loop driven by confidence scores. One tuned agent drafts candidate events, while a second agent scores and refines them round by round. Since no large Indian legal event set existed, they built a synthetic gold set of two thousand cases. The pipeline scores well against that set on a text-match measure. In later tests, a top model preferred timeline-based summaries over plain text in most cases.
arxiv-2603-02051:
Dang-Khoa Le, Hoang-Viet Le, Dai-Nam Le, and colleagues split the motion of a magnetoexciton with no shortcuts at all. Their 2026 work studies excitons, bound pairs of an electron and a hole, in flat materials with a magnetic field. In such materials, mass shifts with direction, so pair motion splits in an uneven way.

Most past work fakes that split with a fixed-form wave, which can skew the pair energy a lot. The team starts from the full energy rule and uses a saved quantity, the pseudomomentum, to split the motion in exact form. New terms that shift with direction show up, which shortcut models miss in full. They then solve the pair rule with a method that homes in step by step. Tests on black phosphorus and titanium trisulfide give pair energies for the ten lowest states.
arxiv-2603-02151:
Darij Grinberg and Benjamin Liber prove a counting claim in this 2026 graph paper. Take a split graph, where nodes fall into two groups with links only across groups. Count its forests, which are link sets with no cycles. Then count the degree lists of all its subgraphs, where each list records links per node.

Shteiner and Shteyner guessed those two counts are always equal for split graphs. Grinberg and Liber prove the guess in full. Along the way, they give several ways to read a key graph score at one point. Those readings use degree lists drawn from directed versions of the graph. The proof ties a pure count of trees to a count of degree patterns.
arxiv-2603-02251:
Carl Mazzanti studies algebraic cycles on a special four-dimensional shape in this 2026 mathematics paper. The shape is the double EPW quartic, a hyperkähler variety first built by Iliev and colleagues. A typical one can also be seen as a moduli space of bundles on a K3 surface. It carries a symmetry that flips its core form, and it links to conic curves in related fourfolds.

Mazzanti uses that rich geometry to test broad conjectures about algebraic cycles. Such conjectures predict how curves and surfaces inside a variety relate to its cycle ring. Hyperkähler varieties are a key test ground, since their cycle behavior is partly mysterious. Double EPW quartics offer enough structure to settle the conjectures in this case.
arxiv-2603-02351:
Leo Kaixuan Cheng, Abdus Shaikh, Ruofan Liang, and colleagues scale up 3D reconstruction in this 2026 paper. New neural models rebuild scenes from photos with high accuracy. Their full attention design, though, eats GPU memory and caps collection size. Large, unordered photo sets simply do not fit.

Their framework, MERG3R, splits the job without any retraining. Photos are reordered and cut into overlapping, varied subsets that fit in memory. Each subset is rebuilt on its own by an existing model. A global alignment step then merges the pieces, weighted by confidence. Across four large benchmarks, accuracy, memory use, and scale all improved. Even a thousand mixed photos yielded solid camera poses and point clouds.
arxiv-2603-02451:
Sheng Sun and Sarah Evans present a framework for trust in distributed AI systems in this 2026 paper. Attestation proves that a system part is what it claims to be. Traditional checks verify a whole system at once, which scales poorly. Systems also change constantly, so one-time checks go stale fast.

Composable attestation verifies parts separately, then combines their proofs. The authors define core properties: proofs must compose, ignore order, and stay deterministic. Merkle trees anchor one construction, with accumulator and multi-signature options also explored. Each option trades speed, security, and features differently. New parts can join through inclusion, without rechecking the whole system. Uses include AI model integrity, federated learning, and live trust assurance.
arxiv-2603-03151:
Qianfeng Li and Emil Wiedemann prove a uniqueness claim for a rigid body in a squeezed, frictionless fluid. Fluid-body problems are hard even for smooth flows. The squeezed, no-friction case had no math results at all before this 2026 paper. Their route lets the fluid's thickness shrink toward zero.

That limit yields a short-time solution of a broad kind, one that can track wiggles and shocks. The main claim is weak-strong uniqueness: when a smooth classic solution exists, the broad one must match it. The proof needs a new trick, since the test shapes used in the no-friction form shift as thickness changes. The result anchors future work on such coupled systems.
arxiv-2603-03251:
Tanishq Kumar, Tri Dao, and Avner May make AI text decoding speculate about its own speculations. Speculative decoding speeds up text output: a fast draft model guesses the next tokens, and a slow target model checks the guesses in one pass. One chain of waiting remains, since drafting waits on checking.

Their new scheme preps drafts for the likely check outcomes while the check still runs. When the real outcome matches a prepped one, that draft returns at once, and drafting costs nothing. The paper names three hurdles this creates and gives principled fixes for each. Their tuned system, Saguaro, ran about thirty percent faster than the best past schemes. Against plain step-by-step decoding, gains reached fivefold.
arxiv-2603-03451:
Luca Previdi and three colleagues push quantum sensing toward measuring several things at once. Near a phase transition, a quantum system becomes hypersensitive, which helps precision, but estimating multiple parameters together usually collapses. The information matrix turns singular, a flaw called sloppiness. Their 2026 paper shows the collapse can be beaten, at a price.

Working with the ground state of the Dicke model, light coupled to atoms in one cavity, they estimate two parameters simultaneously with only mildly reduced precision scaling. A doubled version with photon hopping adds a triple point where two excitation gaps close together. That restores the ideal scaling for chosen parameter pairs. Even with photon loss, steady states keep diverging precision. Preparation time is folded into the comparison of strategies.
arxiv-2603-03551:
Teruki Matsuzaki and three others compute the X-ray fingerprint of a rhenium oxide from first principles. Predicting spectra of correlated quantum substances is hard because spin-orbit coupling, lattice vibration, and electron correlation all tangle jointly. Their 2026 paper applies the formula-of-motion coupled-cluster method, a high-accuracy quantum chemistry tool, to the compound Ba2MgReO6, deriving its spin-orbit-lattice entangled states directly.

The computed interaction parameters land within a few percent of values extracted from real resonant inelastic X-ray scattering spectra. The method also pins down a weak coupling to one vibration family that tests struggle to reach. Simulations show that family creates a shoulder on the elastic peak. Both vibration families prove necessary to reproduce the spectrum's fine structure. The authors present coupled-cluster as a strong predictive tool for such substances.

brown-essays-on-characteristics-1751:
John Brown's Essays on the Characteristics appeared in 1751, aimed at the Earl of Shaftesbury, the most polished thinker of the age. Shaftesbury's Characteristics had taught that taste and good humor could ground morals without revealed religion. Brown, a young clergyman, judged that teaching a danger to faith and public virtue.

The essays charge that Shaftesbury's easy deism saps the roots of both religion and morals. Brown answers wit with argument, testing the earl's claims about virtue, ridicule, and human nature. The orthodox reply made its author famous almost overnight and drew him into print wars with other defenders of Shaftesbury. The book captures a key Enlightenment quarrel: whether manners and taste alone can hold a society together.

Preachers mined the book for centuries, since each tale makes a neat sermon point. Devils tempt, saints rescue, and sinners meet fitting ends. The dialogue frame keeps the lessons lively and plain. This text follows the edition of 1851. Caesarius preserves the most quoted story-hoard of the medieval supernatural, a window on what monks believed, feared, and laughed at.

The energy and devotion of personnel at LINCOLN and the field stations were truly exceptional. Officers are told to pass the credit to the field, where it was earned.
cia-0000137451:
South Vietnamese Liberation Army Enemy Proselyting Office Handling of Prisoners, dated 1971, is a declassified CIA report from the Vietnam War. Its title names its subject in full: how the enemy's proselyting office, the unit charged with winning over captives, handled prisoners it held. Proselyting here means political persuasion work aimed at prisoners of war.

Reports of this kind served a practical purpose. Knowing how captives were treated, and how they were pressed to change sides, shaped briefings for troops and the care of men who came home. The 1971 date places the report in the war's later years, when American forces were drawing down but prisoners remained a live and painful issue.
cia-0000139451: Remote viewing, the attempt to gather intelligence by claimed psychic sight, fills document 0000139451 from Project SUN STREAK in 1988. The program ran under defense and intelligence sponsorship through the 1980s, with viewers set targets they could not see and their reports scored for hits. Nothing in this record sets it apart from the program's general run of files. Freed with the rest of the SUN STREAK archive, it helps show how far officials once went for an edge.
cia-03003751: Early December 1953 produced this daily intelligence bulletin. The third of the month's briefing for policymakers. The Cold War grind, documented. Such papers rarely see the light of day. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
cia-03179151: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1956/03/04, a CIA publication. The March briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06572351: NEW CHILEAN GOVERNMENT LEADERS, a CIA document. The Chilean junta. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
cia-06667951: OS - SCOTT, PAUL <SANITIZED>, a CIA document. The redacted file. This file preserves that declassified paper. It waits for future eyes. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Kept for readers.
ciruelo-reprobacion-supersticiones-spani:
Pedro Ciruelo, a Spanish theologian of the Salamanca school, published his Reprobación de las supersticiones y hechicerías in 1551. The Spanish work condemns popular superstitions and sorceries with strict, measured theology. It became the classic statement of Spanish demonology and shaped the country's theory of witchcraft for generations.

Ciruelo sorts spells, omens, and healers' charms, judging each against church teaching. Much folk practice fails his test, though his temper is cooler than the northern persecutors'. Churchmen quoted him for a full century after his death. The book helps explain why Spain's witch trials took their own, more legalistic course. Salamanca speaks here in its most careful voice.
curieuse-vollstandige-chymische-schrifft: Curieuse vollständige chymische Schrifften, 1751. The curious writings. This book preserves that collection. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Readers can find it here.
europmc-pmc10191851:
Krishna and a large team report that glioblastoma tumors rewire human brain circuits in ways that shorten survival, in a 2023 study. Gliomas are brain tumors that grow into the networks of nerve cells around them. Past work showed that nerve activity feeds tumor growth, and that tumors in turn make nerve cells more excitable.

The team asked whether this rewiring changes how patients fare. They found that tumors which strongly reshape brain circuits are linked to worse survival and poorer thinking skills. The work names brain-tumor crosstalk as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc10248351:
Li and colleagues review inflammation and aging in a 2023 paper, covering signaling pathways and possible interventions. Aging comes with a slow, body-wide rise in inflammation, even without infection. That background inflammation travels with cell aging, immune decline, organ failure, and the diseases of old age.

The review organizes the signals that drive this inflammaging process. It then surveys interventions, from drugs that clear worn-out cells to lifestyle measures. The authors aim to turn a scattered field into a clear map. That map is meant for researchers who seek to slow the harms of aging.
europmc-pmc10477351:
Zhao and co-authors reviewed stromal cells in tumours in 2023, the support cells that frame a cancer's home ground. A tumour's zone holds cancer cells, immune cells, and stromal cells in a shared matrix. Stromal cells can be drawn from nearby healthy tissue. Tumour cells can also turn into stromal-like cells.

These cells feed tumour growth, spread, and drug resistance, Zhao reports. They release growth factors, build new vessels, and reshape the immune tone nearby. Five main kinds get close study, from fibroblasts to fat cells and vessel wall cells. In some settings, though, stromal cells hold a tumour back. That split makes them a tricky but rich drug target.
europmc-pmc10567551:
Sun led the Pharma Proteomics Project report in 2023 on blood proteins in 54,219 UK Biobank members. The project is a shared effort by drug firms and the biobank. It read 2,923 proteins in blood and searched genomes for spots that set each level. Such spots reveal how genes steer the blood's protein mix.

The search found 14,287 main gene links, and 81% were new. Sun also mapped links in people of non-European ancestry. Blood type genes showed long-range effects on gut-linked proteins. The data can test drug targets, such as the cholesterol target PCSK9, on fresh outcomes. All results sit open for any lab to use.
europmc-pmc10766651:
Appelman and co-authors studied muscle harm in long Covid in 2024, centred on crashes after effort. A hallmark of long Covid is post-exertional malaise, a worsening of fatigue and pain after body or mind effort. Its roots have stayed murky. The team ran a case-control study that provoked the crash on purpose.

Muscle build in patients tied to lower exercise capacity, Appelman reports. After the crash was induced, the harm grew worse. Muscle tissue showed strong injury signs and deposits that hold amyloid, a sticky protein. Fuel faults showed in the muscle and in the blood as well. The work maps new paths for grasping the crash state.
europmc-pmc10767851:
Schubach and co-authors released CADD v1.7 in 2024, a tool that scores gene variants for harm. CADD ranks each DNA change by how likely it is to matter for health. Clinics and labs use such ranks to sort finds. The tool has been honed since its first release years ago.

New inputs lift its calls, Schubach reports. They include protein language model scores, gene control forecasts from neural nets, and fresh conservation scores from the Zoonomia project. Tests used disease data banks and 31 deep lab scans of protein changes. Scores for the whole genome sit free on the project site. A web server lets any user score a variant on site.
europmc-pmc11217151:
Smolka and a large team present a faster, sharper tool for finding large genome changes in this 2024 paper. Structural variants are DNA changes of 50 letters or more, and they are hard to call accurately. Long reads remain the most accurate way to spot complex changes. Their tool, Sniffles2, improves the search with repeat-aware clustering and coverage-adaptive filtering.

Sniffles2 ran 11.8 times faster and 29 percent more accurate than leading callers, the authors report. Tests spanned low to high coverage and two sequencing technologies. It also calls variants jointly across families and populations, producing fully genotyped files. In 11 patients it found the causative changes near a key gene, including one allele with three overlapping changes. It even detected mosaic changes, present in only some cells, in brain tissue.
europmc-pmc11369751:
Efthimiou, Seo, Chalkou, Debray, Egger, and Salanti write a step-by-step guide to building clinical prediction models in this 2024 paper. Prediction models forecast a patient's future health from baseline traits and guide medical decisions. Many are published each year, yet evidence shows published studies often carry severe methodological flaws. Those flaws undermine the models' usefulness.

The guide walks through defining the aim and the intended users first. It then covers choosing data sources, handling missing data, and weighing modelling options. Assessing model performance closes the workflow. Steps are illustrated with an example from relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, a disease with flare-ups and remissions. Full R code accompanies the guide. The authors aim to raise the standard of a crowded literature.
europmc-pmc11701551:
Blum and a large team report the 2025 status of InterPro, a protein sequence classification resource, in this paper. InterPro sorts protein sequences into families. It merges predictive models, called signatures, from many member databases to predict domains and key sites in a sequence. Its annotations cover more than 200 million sequences.

Coverage spans UniProtKB, the main protein sequence archive, with links to the Gene Ontology, the European structure bank PDBe, and the AlphaFold structure database. Version 101.0 is detailed, with its website and software. More than 5,000 new entries were created in the past two years. Use of AlphaFold-predicted structures grew, and AI now helps write family descriptions. The site gives access to 85 member collections.
europmc-pmc1180851:
Durán and co-authors described in 2005 how a common fungus can make tiny silver particles. The fungus is Fusarium oxysporum, a microbe found in soil and plants. When silver ions in water meet the fungus, the ions change form. Solid silver particles then appear outside the fungal cells.

Those particles measured about 20 to 50 nanometers across. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter. Durán points to an enzyme and to small shuttle molecules as the drivers. The method offers a cleaner way to make silver material that can kill bacteria.
europmc-pmc1241351:
Perera and colleagues linked prenatal pollution exposure to birth outcomes in 2003. Inner-city minority families face high rates of poor birth outcomes. They also face more smoke, hydrocarbons, and pesticides. The sample held 263 nonsmoking African-American and Dominican women.

Personal air monitors tracked hydrocarbon exposure during pregnancy. Blood measures captured tobacco smoke and a common pesticide. Among African-American mothers, high hydrocarbon exposure tied to lower birth weight. It also tied to smaller head size at birth. The pesticide measure tied to lower weight and shorter length overall. Perera shows womb exposure can shrink newborns. Most women were tracked with home air samplers and blood tests. Most of the women lived in New York City. Their births took place in city hospitals. Birth weight was the main size check used in the work.
europmc-pmc1413551:
Swollen, active immune cells in the spinal cord may drive harm in two nerve diseases. Yiangou and co-authors checked human spinal cord tissue after death in 2006. They looked at multiple sclerosis, which attacks nerve insulation, and ALS, which kills motor nerve cells. They stained for three proteins tied to inflammation: COX-2, CB2, and P2X7.

Control cords showed few stained cells. Cords from both diseases held far more, with longer arms, in the hurt zones. Yiangou used scans and blots to confirm the rise. The shared pattern hints that calming these cells could help in both diseases.
europmc-pmc1636651:
A simple score can flag fatty liver without an ultrasound. Bedogni and co-authors built the Fatty Liver Index in 2006 from an Italian population study. Fatty liver is the most common liver disease in Western countries. They tested 13 candidate predictors in about 500 people.

Four measures did the job: body mass index, waist size, triglycerides, and one liver enzyme, GGT. The index runs from 0 to 100 with an accuracy of 0.84. Below 30, fatty liver is ruled out; at 60 or above, it is ruled in. Bedogni offers it to target scans and lifestyle advice.
europmc-pmc1660551:
Two gene families take up a tenth of the TB germ's genome, yet their jobs are unknown. Gey van Pittius and co-authors traced their evolution in 2006. The PE and PPE families have been tied to antigen variation and disease.

Their growth links to duplication of the ESAT-6 gene clusters, regions that export potent immune targets. Copies inside those clusters are the families' oldest members. Two repeat subfamilies arose recently, only in the TB complex and close kin. Gey van Pittius mapped all PE and PPE genes across sequenced Mycobacterium genomes, clarifying how this large, mysterious family expanded.
europmc-pmc2130951: A medical paper on focal interstitial nephritis in the calf after interference with normal function. The calf kidney. This article preserves that veterinary nephrology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2131651: A medical paper on the liver as the source of fibrinogen. The clotting source. This article preserves that physiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2147051:
Benner and colleagues reported in 2008 that immune responses to altered alpha-synuclein speed brain cell loss in a Parkinson's model. Parkinson's disease kills dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra. Their clumps contain nitrated alpha-synuclein, a protein changed by oxidative damage. The team asked whether that change creates targets for the adaptive immune system. They used mice poisoned with MPTP, a toxin that mimics the disease.

Nitrated protein appeared in neck lymph nodes, where presenting cells ramped up display machinery. MPTP-treated mice made antibodies against normal and nitrated protein. Immunising mice with the nitrated fragment produced strong T cell responses specific to the modified form. Mice lacking T and B cells resisted MPTP damage. Transferring those T cells accelerated dopamine neuron loss. Tolerance to the altered protein can thus break and worsen disease.
europmc-pmc2323751: Red blood cells burst when complement gets going, and this opening paper made the case that fixation drives the hemolysis. Experiments traced the destructive sequence. The immune system's bursting mechanism, detailed. The article preserves that immunology research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2360651:
Maggi and co-authors compared two follow-up treatments for high-risk womb cancer in a 2006 randomised trial. The cancer, endometrial carcinoma, grows in the womb lining. After surgery, patients at high risk of return get either radiation or chemotherapy, and no one knew which worked better.

The trial assigned 345 patients to radiation or to a three-drug chemotherapy plan given five times. After a median follow-up of about 95 months, survival was nearly the same in both groups. At seven years, 62% of patients were alive in each group. Radiation delayed cancer returning near the pelvis, while chemotherapy delayed spread to distant sites, but neither trend was strong enough to count as proven. The authors said neither treatment won, and trials combining both were needed.
europmc-pmc2386051:
Oldfield and colleagues examined floppy protein regions as social tools in 2008. Some proteins lack a fixed shape and fold only when they grab a partner, a property called intrinsic disorder. Hub proteins, which bind many partners, may use that flexibility as a net that fits many shapes.

They studied two opposite cases in detail. The tumor guard p53 uses several floppy regions, and single regions of it can bind many different partners. The protein 14-3-3 is the reverse: rigid itself, but it binds many floppy partners. Structures of their complexes showed both tricks at work: disordered regions moulding to fit, and even firm regions reshaping slightly on contact, called induced fit. The authors said disorder gives hub proteins their binding range, with induced fit fine-tuning each grip.
europmc-pmc2429951:
Genton and co-authors followed malaria cases at two rural health centres in Papua New Guinea in 2008. Severe malaria was classically blamed on one parasite species, falciparum, while vivax was thought mild. Some hints even suggested mixed infections protect patients, and this eight-year surveillance tested those beliefs.

Of 17,201 suspected cases, 9,537 had confirmed parasites in their blood. About 6.2% of confirmed cases met the World Health Organization definition of severe malaria, most of them children under five. In that age group, severe disease struck 11.7% of falciparum cases, 8.8% of vivax cases, and 17.3% of mixed infections, so mixing gave no protection. Vivax cases showed breathing distress more often than falciparum cases, at 60% versus 41%, but anaemia less often. The authors warned that falciparum-only programs would miss much severe disease.
europmc-pmc2583951:
Müller and colleagues searched in 2008 for the enzyme that lets wild malaria mosquitoes in Ghana survive pyrethroid insecticides. Resistance threatens the spraying and bednet programmes holding malaria back in Africa. The team measured activity of over 250 detoxification genes in individual mosquitoes from a highly resistant wild population, comparing survivors of insecticide exposure with the rest.

One gene stood out: CYP6P3, a cytochrome P450 enzyme, was produced far more in the survivors. The team then made the enzyme in the lab. It breaks down pyrethroids directly, both the alpha-cyano and non-alpha-cyano types. This was the first proof of something key. A P450 found overactive in wild Anopheles gambiae can actually break down the insecticides. The finding supports simple monitoring tools that watch for this gene's activity.
europmc-pmc2592351:
Fazel, Khosla, Doll, and Geddes systematically reviewed in 2008 how common major mental disorders are among homeless people in Western countries. Over a million people are homeless across Western Europe and North America, yet pooled prevalence figures were lacking. The authors searched for interview-based surveys of unselected homeless samples and combined 29 studies covering 5,684 people in seven countries.

Alcohol dependence was the most common disorder, ranging from 8.1 percent to 58.5 percent across studies, followed by drug dependence at 4.5 percent to 54.2 percent in the samples. Psychotic illness ranged from 2.8 percent to 42.3 percent, with major depression showing similar spread. Estimates varied far more than chance allows, and alcohol dependence had grown more common in recent decades. The authors conclude homeless people carry far higher rates than the general population.
europmc-pmc2621351:
Hastings, Ira, and Lupski proposed in 2009 a mechanism explaining how the genome gains and loses chunks of DNA, creating copy number variation behind many genomic disorders. Their clue came from duplications in Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. Those events showed three odd features. Most were complex mixtures of duplications, deletions, and inversions. The junctions shared tiny 2 to 5 letter matches, called microhomology. The endpoints clustered near repeated DNA stretches.

Their model, named microhomology-mediated break-induced replication, starts when a DNA copying fork breaks in a stressed cell. The loose strand end latches onto any nearby single strand sharing a few matching letters and restarts copying sloppily, switching templates repeatedly. The result is exactly the complex, scrambled rearrangements observed, and over time this process may even build the repeats themselves.
europmc-pmc2643051:
Yu-Wai-Man and colleagues reviewed in 2009 two inherited eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, the cable carrying signals from eye to brain. Both strike mainly young adults. One, called LHON, follows faults in the DNA of mitochondria, the cell's energy makers. The other, called DOA, usually follows faults in a gene named OPA1, which helps mitochondria work.

In both diseases the cells that die are retinal ganglion cells, whose fibers form the optic nerve. Why these cells suffer most, when the gene faults sit in every cell, remains a key puzzle. The review covers what is known about family patterns, why some carriers stay healthy, and how the damage unfolds. Knowing the weak points, the authors argue, is the first step toward treatments, which are still lacking.
europmc-pmc2656551:
Gaillard and co-authors recorded brain signals in 2009 from inside the skulls of ten patients to find what marks a word becoming conscious. Some words were flashed and then masked, so patients never noticed them. Others were shown clearly. Electrodes placed for medical care let the team watch both kinds of processing directly.

Masked words still stirred activity in several brain areas, but only briefly and locally, like a wave that dies out. Words seen on purpose looked very different. Four signs converged on the same moments. Lasting voltage shifts appeared, strong in the front of the brain. Fast gamma waves rose sharply. Distant areas pulsed in step, and far-apart regions clearly influenced each other. The authors argue these are four windows on a single state: a brain-wide pattern that holds the word in awareness.
europmc-pmc2699551:
Abbas and colleagues used in 2009 a mathematical unmixing technique to read the cell traffic inside blood samples from lupus patients. Lupus is an autoimmune disease with a shifting cast of blood cell changes, which ordinary gene readings blur together. Their method, expression deconvolution, teases a mixed sample's signal apart into the voices of its cell types.

First the team proved the method on real blood and on lab-made mixtures, where it recovered the true proportions. Applied to lupus, it found a broad activation pattern: monocytes, natural killer cells, and helper T cells all expanded and switched on together. These shifts partly explain the disease's famous interferon signature, a gene pattern long observed but unassigned. The patterns tracked how sick patients were and what treatment they received. Cell-level bookkeeping of this kind, the authors argue, turns a blood sample into a census of the disease.
europmc-pmc2703651:
Androutsopoulos, Tsatsakis, and Spandidos reviewed in 2009 the wider roles of CYP1A1, an enzyme that breaks down foreign chemicals in the body. The enzyme sits mostly outside the liver and is switched on by smoke and other pollutants through a sensor called AhR. For years it was known chiefly for turning some chemicals into forms that can cause cancer.

Their review weighs newer proof that CYP1A1 can also clear harmful chemicals and unlock helpful compounds in food that may guard against cancer. AhR also affects cell growth and death, not just chemical breakdown. Whether CYP1A1 helps or harms, they argue, depends on which of these jobs wins out in a given tissue.
europmc-pmc2705351:
Hofvander and co-authors described in 2009 the mental health and daily life of adults with autism spectrum disorders who have normal intelligence. Autism affects social contact and speech and nonverbal cues. Most outcome studies had focused on children or on people with added learning disability, leaving this adult group less known.

They assessed 122 adults seen in clinic, most with Asperger disorder or a related form. Core autism traits were common in all groups, and lifetime mood and anxiety problems were very common too. Few led an independent life, and very few had held a long-term relationship, which shows high support needs in adult life.
europmc-pmc2778451:
Alvarez and Ashraf reviewed in 2010 the role of vitamin D in insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity, the two processes that govern blood sugar. Vitamin D is known for bone health, but evidence hints it also protects the cells that make insulin and the tissues that answer it. They gathered cross-sectional, prospective, and intervention studies on vitamin D and glucose control.

Blood levels of the vitamin D marker ran inversely with insulin resistance in snapshot studies, though direct sensitivity measures are still needed. Reports on insulin secretion conflicted with each other. Prospective studies supported a protective effect of high levels against type 2 diabetes. Trial results were inconsistent overall, likely due to differing populations, study lengths, and supplement forms. They call for trials in people at high risk of both vitamin D deficiency and diabetes.
europmc-pmc2813751:
Liu, Fowler, Smith, and Dalgleish tested in 2010 whether standard chemotherapy can make tumors easier for the immune system to attack. Chemo drugs were long assumed to clash with immune therapy because they also harm immune cells. The team treated tumor cells with three common drugs and watched a display protein called HLA class 1, which flags cells for killing.

The drugs raised HLA display on tumor cells, even where it started low, and killer T cells then destroyed more of them. Blocking HLA erased that gain. Liquid from drug-treated tumors also matured dendritic cells, the scouts that train T cells, and T-cell growth rose. The findings suggest some chemo restores a slice of immune surveillance.
europmc-pmc2876151:
Enserink and Kolodner reviewed in 2010 the targets of Cdk1, the master enzyme that drives cells through division in budding yeast. Cdk1 is a cyclin-dependent kinase, an enzyme switched on by partner proteins called cyclins. A decade of work had pinned down roughly seventy-five proteins it modifies to run the division cycle.

Those targets control copying the DNA, separating the copied chromosomes, switching gene programs, and shaping the dividing cell. Several also guard genome stability, repairing damage and checking that copying finished before division starts. By modifying each target at the right moment, one enzyme sequences the whole cycle in order. The review organizes the target list by job and flags where human cell division uses the same logic.
europmc-pmc2893951:
Kilkenny, Browne, Cuthill, Emerson, and Altman introduced in 2010 the ARRIVE guidelines for reporting animal research, modeled on the checklists that cleaned up clinical trial reports. Reviews had shown that papers routinely omit basic facts, such as how animals were assigned to groups, whether assessors were blinded, and how group sizes were chosen. Without those facts, readers cannot judge a study and funders' money is wasted.

The guidelines list the essential items every animal study report should state, from design and animal details to full statistical methods. They were built with input from scientists, journal editors, and funders, and journals began requiring the checklist at submission. The aim is simple: an animal experiment should be reported completely enough for others to repeat and trust it.
europmc-pmc2910551:
Balistreri, Caruso, and Candore reviewed in 2010 how body fat acts as an endocrine organ whose signals fan chronic inflammation across the body. Fat tissue releases adipokines, hormone-like messengers that reach the liver, vessels, and immune system. In obesity, over a billion people are overweight worldwide and more than three hundred million are obese, the balance of those messengers tips toward inflammation.

The review traces how the pro-inflammatory tilt feeds the diseases that travel with obesity, including insulin resistance, fatty liver, vessel disease, and some cancers. Individual adipokines get full treatment: leptin and adiponectin, the best-known pair, plus newer names from fat-resident immune cells. Understanding fat as a signaling organ reframes obesity treatment from calorie bookkeeping toward calming a body-wide inflammatory state.
europmc-pmc2920551:
Wiese and colleagues reviewed in 2010 saxitoxin and its fifty-seven chemical cousins, the paralytic shellfish toxins that close beaches and poison seafood eaters. The toxins are made by ocean dinoflagellates and by freshwater cyanobacteria during blooms. They block nerve signals, so poisoning can paralyze breathing muscles within hours of a contaminated meal.

The analogs sort into structural classes, from unsulfated to doubly sulfated and greasy variants, each with its own potency. Shellfish, bacteria, and even the human body convert one analog into another, sometimes softening and sometimes sharpening toxicity. Tracing those conversions matters twice over. It predicts how long a harvest stays dangerous. It also hints at detox methods for contaminated shellfish and drinking water. The review maps both active goals.
europmc-pmc2923151:
Dumas and co-authors recorded in 2010 two brains at once to catch the neural signature of people falling into sync during social interaction. Nine pairs of participants took turns imitating each other's hand movements spontaneously, switching leader and follower freely, while dual EEG headsets captured both brains. Interactional synchrony, the smooth mutual adaptation of partners, is the bedrock of conversation and joint play.

When behavioral synchrony peaked, a synchronizing network emerged between the two brains in the alpha-mu rhythm band, linking right centroparietal regions on both sides. The coupling rose and fell with the quality of the interaction rather than with movement alone. Brains literally tune to each other during real exchange, the authors argue, giving social neuroscience a measurable inter-brain phenomenon to study.
europmc-pmc2930851:
Studerus, Gamma, and Vollenweider tested a long-used questionnaire for altered states of consciousness in a 2010 psychometric study. The OAV scale had served researchers for over twenty years, yet its factor structure had never faced strict statistical testing.

Pooling data from forty-three experiments, they covered several hundred sessions involving psilocybin, ketamine, or MDMA. Modern modelling showed the original factor plan fit poorly, and two broad factors could merge at a higher level. The team instead drew out eleven narrower factors and checked how drug type and other causes shaped scores, giving future studies a firmer scale.
europmc-pmc2973851:
Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux introduced a method for uncovering genetic clusters in populations in a 2010 article, designed for the flood of data from fast sequencing. Popular model-based clustering tools strain under huge datasets because they lean on heavy assumptions and computing.

Their method first compresses genetic data into principal components, then seeks the grouping that best separates clusters while keeping members tight. When groups are unknown, a repeated grouping routine proposes them. Tested on simulated data against a leading program, it recovered structure well and also supplies membership scores, visual separation, and which gene variants drive the split.
europmc-pmc2976751:
Liu, Yu, and Edwards developed a statistical shortcut for estimating species family trees from many gene trees in a 2010 article. Gene histories legitimately differ inside a species tree, and the exact best-fit calculation for the standard model turns out not to exist.

Their substitute scores candidate trees with a pseudo-likelihood, an approximation they prove settles on the truth as gene counts grow. Simulations confirm the approach even in a tricky zone where gene trees commonly mislead. Applied to mammals, it recovered the same four major groupings as a rival method, with stronger support values in places.
europmc-pmc2990751:
Hoshida presented nearest template prediction, a method for classifying a single patient's gene activity profile, in a 2010 article. Gene signature tests had stalled before reaching clinics because measurements vary between labs and platforms, and most methods judge batches rather than individuals.

Given only a list of signature genes and one sample, the method assigns a class and computes a confidence score for that call. Tests showed it working across platforms, across species, and with several classes at once, without tuning settings for each dataset. That flexibility targets the practical barriers holding back bedside use.
europmc-pmc3004851:
Charlson and colleagues sequenced airway bacteria from healthy smokers and non-smokers in a 2010 study, asking how smoking reshapes whole microbial communities rather than single species. Smokers suffer more airway infections, for reasons only partly explained.

Samples from both sides of the nose and throat in sixty-two adults yielded hundreds of thousands of gene reads. Community makeup depended mainly on airway site, yet smokers' communities were more diverse and grouped apart from non-smokers'. Several bacterial groups shifted consistently with smoking, and the throat gained anaerobic types tied to gum disease. The work gives a baseline map of the smoker's airway.
europmc-pmc3069751:
Murshudov and coauthors explained in 2011 the principles behind REFMAC5, the program most CCP4 users rely on to refine crystal structures. Refinement adjusts an atomic model until it best matches the measured diffraction data while staying chemically sensible. The program has been a suite staple for years, and this paper gathers its design in one place.

It covers how the program balances data fit against prior knowledge of bond lengths and angles. It also covers handling of disorder and partial occupancy, and treatment of low resolution and twinned data. Restraints drawn from known small molecule chemistry keep models plausible where data are weak. The authors also describe validation checks that flag overfitting. For practicing crystallographers, the paper is the reference for what the program is doing during its many cycles, and why its settings matter.
europmc-pmc3082551:
Braidy, Guillemin, Mansour, Chan-Ling, Poljak, and Grant tracked in 2011 how aging drains a key metabolic cofactor in rat organs, with knock on effects for stress defense. The cofactor, NAD in its charged form, fuels energy chemistry and also feeds enzymes that guard DNA and control aging programs. The team measured it and related markers in heart, lung, liver, and kidney from young and middle aged female rats.

By middle age, cofactor levels and balance had fallen significantly in every organ. Damage markers from oxidation rose in step, total antioxidant capacity fell, and DNA damage tags accumulated. The activity of a longevity linked enzyme that depends on the cofactor dropped, while the power stations of the cells ran weaker across the board. The tight match between DNA damage and cofactor loss suggests keeping levels up may be one key to healthy aging.
europmc-pmc3094351:
O'Donovan and colleagues reported in 2011 on older adults carrying a heavy combined load of two inflammatory signals. Those adults were more likely to have short chromosome caps in their white blood cells. Short caps, called telomeres, mark biological aging, and chronic inflammation is suspected of wearing them down. The team studied nearly two thousand well functioning adults in their seventies in a long running aging study.

People high on either of two inflammation markers had higher odds of short caps. People high on both had higher odds still, beyond either alone, after accounting for many other risk factors. A third common marker, C reactive protein, showed no such link. The authors call this the first large scale evidence tying cumulative inflammation to telomere shortening in older adults. It supports the idea that quiet, long running inflammation helps drive the aging of immune cells.
europmc-pmc3118151:
Jorma Panula and colleagues tracked deaths after hip fracture surgery in older Finns in a 2011 study in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. Hip fractures are the gravest result of falls in old age, and death rates after them are known to be high. The team followed more than four hundred patients aged sixty-five and over and compared them with the general older population.

About a quarter of patients died within a year of surgery, and most had died by the end of follow-up. Death rates ran about three times higher than in the general population, across every major cause, with heart and circulation diseases first, then dementia. europmc-pmc3121651:
Jane Achan and colleagues reviewed the place of quinine in malaria care in a 2011 paper in Malaria Journal. The drug, drawn from tree bark used in South America in the sixteen hundreds, was the first chemical cure for an infectious disease. Nearly four centuries on, it remains in use, though newer drugs beat it in several settings.

For severe malaria, injected artesunate should now come first, with quinine as a backup. In pregnancy, especially early on, quinine still plays a central role until safer options exist. For mild illness, combined artemisinin treatments work better, but supply gaps in poor regions make dropping quinine risky. The authors advise fixing supply chains and watching for clashes with HIV and tuberculosis drugs.
europmc-pmc3127851:
Marianne Sinka and colleagues mapped the main malaria-carrying mosquitoes of the Asia-Pacific region in a 2011 paper in Malaria Journal. The region hosts many such species at once, often in look-alike groups with flexible behaviour, which makes control unusually hard. This paper closed a three-part world survey of dominant malaria vectors.

The team combined expert range maps with records gathered from published sources, covering more than ten thousand places across thirty-one countries. Modelled maps were produced for each of nineteen dominant species, alongside plain-language summaries of each species' habits and ecology. The result is a reference intended to sharpen species-specific control and guide further study of mosquito biology in the region where malaria control faces its most tangled vector problem.
europmc-pmc3138751:
Marc Jeschke and colleagues followed severely burned children for three years in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Deep burns trigger sweeping metabolic upheaval, but how long the body stays in that crisis state was unknown. Nearly a thousand children burned over almost a third of their bodies were tracked at a specialist centre and compared with uninjured children.

Resting energy burn, body composition, heart and organ function, and blood markers all stayed clearly abnormal for the full three years. Stress hormones and inflammatory signals also stayed high, showing a prolonged overdrive state rather than a brief reaction. The authors argue care and nutrition support for severe burns must extend far beyond hospital discharge, reshaping follow-up plans for young patients.
europmc-pmc3141051:
Erik Gullberg and colleagues showed that vanishingly weak antibiotics still breed resistant bacteria in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Drug resistance is usually blamed on treatment doses, yet bacteria also meet faint traces of drugs in soil, water, and waste. Using sensitive head-to-head growth contests, the team asked how faint a drug level can still favour resistant strains.

For three major antibiotics, levels hundreds of times below those needed to stop normal bacteria still let resistant ones take over, even when they started rare. Brand-new resistant mutants also arose and were picked out at these low levels. A mathematical model predicts how fast such mutants would sweep a normal population. The results argue that faint environmental drug pollution matters for the resistance crisis.
europmc-pmc3203851:
Jacob Durrant and J. Andrew McCammon reviewed molecular dynamics simulations in drug discovery in this 2011 article in BMC Biology. These simulations track the atoms of a protein and a candidate drug molecule as they move over time. The authors survey the many points in a drug project where such simulations can help.

Simulations can reveal hidden binding pockets that static structures miss, including sites away from the main active site. They can sharpen virtual screening, the computer sifting of huge compound libraries, and they can directly estimate how tightly a molecule will bind. The authors are candid about limits: the calculations are expensive and rely on approximations of physical forces. Even so, with faster computers and better algorithms, they expect simulations to matter more and more.
europmc-pmc3237351:
Shannon Levesque and colleagues examined how diesel exhaust inflames the brain in this 2011 study in Environmental Health Perspectives. Air pollution is linked to brain disease, but the mechanism was unclear. The team exposed rats to diesel exhaust and tested exhaust particles on cell cultures, looking for effects on microglia, the brain's immune cells, and on dopamine neurons.

Inhaled exhaust raised inflammatory markers across most brain regions, with the midbrain responding most strongly, and particles injected into the airway activated microglia near dopamine pathways. In culture, particles alone caused little cytokine output, but they primed microglia so a later bacterial stimulus triggered an exaggerated response that harmed dopamine neurons. A protective signal, fractalkine, softened some of that damage. The findings outline how pollution could stoke neuroinflammation.
europmc-pmc3257651:
Philip Calder reviewed omega-3 fatty acids and inflammation in this 2010 article in Nutrients. The long-chain fats in oily fish influence inflammation through several routes, most of them running through the fatty makeup of cell membranes. Changing that makeup alters membrane fluidity, cell signaling and gene activity, and which lipid messengers a cell produces.

Inflammatory cells are normally rich in the omega-6 fat arachidonic acid, whose messenger products promote inflammation. Eating the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA displaces some of it, and the messengers made from them often act differently, some actively resolving inflammation; these resolvins were a recent discovery. Membrane changes also affect peptide signals such as cytokines and adhesion molecules. Calder concludes the marine omega-3s may serve as treatments for disorders with an inflammatory component.
europmc-pmc3369951:
Schwartz and colleagues reported in 2012 that Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that colonizes skin, builds fibers to hold its biofilms together. Biofilms are sticky surface communities behind many stubborn infections. The fibers turned out to be made of small peptides called phenol soluble modulins.

Lab tests showed the peptides clump into amyloid-like fibers with classic amyloid traits. Mutant germs unable to make them fell apart when enzymes or physical stress attacked the biofilm. Loose peptides scattered biofilms, while the clumped form did the opposite. The switch helps explain how the germ balances holding on and spreading.
europmc-pmc3404651:
Dodson and a team tested hundreds of consumer products in 2012 for chemicals that disrupt hormones or aggravate asthma. They bought more than two hundred products across fifty types, from cosmetics and cleaners to sunscreens and vinyl goods.

Some products swapped well-known problem chemicals for less-studied cousins with similar effects. Many detected chemicals never appeared on labels at all. Smarter shopping can dodge some, the authors say, but fuller labeling is needed.

fielding-amelia-1751:
Amelia, published in 1751, was Fielding's last novel, and his most serious. It draws on the troubles of his own first marriage and his years as a London magistrate. Many readers rank its heroine among the finest women in early fiction.

Amelia Booth stays loyal to her husband Billy, a charming, weak ex-officer ruined by debt, drink, and prison. Fielding shows the sponging houses, bailiffs, and corrupt courts that ground the poor of London. The tone is tender and angry at once. Amelia sold more slowly than Tom Jones, but later critics, Dickens among them, praised its truth and pathos.
finney-systematic-theology-1851:
Finney's Lectures on Systematic Theology, published in 1851, give the Oberlin evangelist's complete doctrinal system in his own words. Finney taught theology at Oberlin College in Ohio, where his revival preaching had already reshaped American evangelical life. The lectures were his classroom teaching, set down in full.

His system is known as moral-government theology: God rules as a moral governor, and sinners can repent because the will is truly free. Finney argues point by point against the stricter Calvinism in which he had been raised. The book remains the fullest statement of Oberlin theology and of revivalist doctrine.
firmicus-maternus-mathesis-1551: Julius Firmicus Maternus's Mathesis, in this 1551 Latin edition, is the great Roman handbook of astrology. The 4th-century author lays out how the stars were read to foretell a life. It is the fullest surviving guide to how Rome practiced the art.
firmicus-maternus-mathesis-latin-1551:
Julius Firmicus Maternus wrote Rome's fullest handbook of the stars in the fourth century. Mathesis, in the Latin printing of 1551, gives his eight books in their old form. The 1551 edition is a fine Renaissance print of a late Roman work.

Firmicus teaches the whole art of casting a birth chart: planets, houses, lots, and the fates read from them. He mixes hard rules with praise of the star craft and scorn for its frauds. No Latin book of astrology to survive matches its scope. The old print lets readers meet the work as Renaissance scholars did.
five-treatises-of-the-philosophers-stone: Five Treatises of the Philosophers Stone, 1651. The five treatises. This book preserves that collection. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
frus-1861-d151:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 September 1861. The dispatch is document 151 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's early September report keeps the Paris watch at its steady pace. He had learned the court's moods and could read small signs. Washington drew on that feel when it judged how far French patience with the war might stretch. Feel for a court cannot be taught by cable, and Dayton had it in full. Feel for a court is the one tool no office at home could supply by mail.
frus-1861-d251:
The home office spoke to James Shepherd Pike on 5 September 1861, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 251 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d51:
On 8 June 1861, William H. Seward sent a brief letter to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 51 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward sent Adams frequent, brief direction through the summer of 1861. Each letter dealt with the point then at hand, from notes to claims. This June note is one stroke in a run of orders that kept London's envoy and Washington's chief in close step despite the slow mails. Brief orders suited Adams, who liked clear tasks and disliked loose talk in state papers. Clear tasks also let Adams answer fast when a point turned hot in talks.
frus-1862-d151:
From London on 25 September 1862, Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. Adams was the American minister to Britain, and his reports home appear throughout the 1862 Foreign Relations volume; this one is Document 151.

An envoy's report mixed what he had done, what officials had said to him, and what the press and public seemed to think. Seward read these London letters to judge the risk that Britain might back the Confederacy or push for a truce. Reports like this one were the government's eyes in the capital that mattered most. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d251:
On 3 February 1862 William L. Dayton wrote from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward, in a report printed as Document 251 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton had served as American minister to France since 1861.

Early February brought the fall of Fort Henry in Tennessee, the first big Union win of the year. Such news mattered in Paris, where bets on the war's length guided French choices. Dayton's reports mixed court talk with press and market reaction, giving Seward the raw material for his replies to the French legation in Washington. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d351:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward closed the year with a letter to Henri Mercier dated 31 December 1861, printed as Document 351 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier was France's minister in Washington.

New Year's Eve 1861 found the Trent crisis settled and French, British, and Spanish troops landing in Mexico. Seward faced a year ahead in which France would test American patience on two fronts. His year-end letter to Mercier is a fitting close to the French file's first chapter: courteous in form, careful in substance. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d451:
On 17 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley at the legation in Vienna. The instruction is Document 451 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

February brought Union victories at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson, and Seward was quick to put such news in his ministers' hands. Motley in Vienna had to counter a court press that often took the Confederacy's side. Orders from Washington gave him the facts and the argument: the rebellion was failing, and foreign backing for it would be wasted. The letter is one move in the paper campaign the Union fought in every European capital that winter.
frus-1862-d51:
From abroad on 24 April 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 51 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d551:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1862. His note is Document 551 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

October brought the Dutch minister a Washington calmer than September's, with Lee back in Virginia and the intervention scare cooling. Van Limburg's note took up the standing business of his legation, which centered on Dutch trade and the treatment of neutral shipping. The Netherlands file in the volume never rises to crisis, and that is its historical value. It records the normal temperature of relations between the Union and a friendly maritime power. It does so in the middle of a civil war.
frus-1862-d651:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this letter to Townsend Harris on 23 July 1861. Harris was the American minister in Japan, the man who had won the 1858 trade treaty with the shogun's court. The letter is document 651 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Seward's letters to his envoys carried orders, news from home, and the line each post was to take. This one went out in the first summer of the Civil War, when Washington had few men and little money to spare for far-off posts. It shows the State Department still steering its Japan mission week by week, even with a war on.
frus-1863p1-d151:
